sceneHappening: Bearing with one another, Christ the servant of all, and Paul's plans for Rome and Spain
summary: "Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up. For even Christ didn't please himself. But, as it is written, 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.'" For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of perseverance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind one with another according to Christ Jesus, that with one accord you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. "Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God." Christ has become a servant to the circumcision for the truth of God, that he might confirm the promises given to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. Paul strings together quotations: "Therefore I will give praise to you among the Gentiles," "Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people," "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles," "There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope." "Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope, in the power of the Holy Spirit." He says he is persuaded that they are full of goodness and able to admonish one another, and that he has written to them boldly in part, as putting them in mind, because of the grace given to him by God, "that I should be a servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving as a priest the Good News of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles may be made acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Spirit." He has reason to boast in Christ Jesus, in things pertaining to God; he dares to speak only of what Christ has accomplished through him, by word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God, so that from Jerusalem, and around as far as Illyricum, he has fully preached the Good News of Christ. He has made it his aim to preach the Good News where Christ has not been named, that he might not build on another's foundation, as it is written, "They will see, to whom no news of him came, and they who haven't heard will understand." This is why he has often been hindered from coming to them, but now, no longer having any place in these regions, and having these many years a longing to come to them, he hopes to see them in passing as he goes to Spain, and to be helped on his journey there by them, after he has first enjoyed their company for a while. "But now, I say, I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints. For it has been the good pleasure of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem. Yes, it has been their good pleasure, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them to serve them also in fleshly things." When he has completed this, he will go on by way of them to Spain, and he knows that when he comes, he will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ. "Now I beg you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in your prayers to God for me, that I may be delivered from those who are disobedient in Judea, and that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints; that I may come to you in joy through the will of God, and together with you find rest. Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen."
whySettingMatters: Chapter 15 completes the practical section and begins to reveal why Paul wrote. He wraps up the issue of the weak and strong by pointing to Christ, who "did not please himself" (quoting Psalm 69:9), and who became a servant to the Jews for the sake of God's promises and the Gentiles' sake for God's mercy; four quotations from Deuteronomy, the Psalms, and Isaiah show that the Gentile inclusion was always in Scripture. Paul describes his own work in priestly language: "serving as a priest" (hierourgountes), with the Gentiles as his offering, a picture drawn from temple worship. Illyricum was the Roman province across the Adriatic from Italy (modern Albania and Croatia), and it is not mentioned in Acts; Paul's claim that he has "fully preached" from Jerusalem to Illyricum means he has established churches in the main cities. His plan for Spain was to open a western mission; he asks the Romans to "send him on his way," meaning provide support. The collection for the poor in Jerusalem, taken from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia, is described in 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 8 and 9; Paul sees it as a way of binding Gentile and Jewish believers, and he is anxious about both the risk in Judea and whether the gift will be accepted. Acts 24:17 mentions the gift. How the plans turned out is told in Acts: Paul reached Rome as a prisoner. Whether he reached Spain is not recorded, and is debated.

questions: "Christ did not please himself." How does that shape what Paul asks of the strong?
Paul calls his ministry "serving as a priest" and his Gentile converts an offering. What does that picture give to his work?
The collection ties Gentile churches to Jewish believers in Jerusalem. What is Paul hoping it will do?
Paul asks the Romans to pray for him to be rescued in Judea. How does that sit with his confident plans?
